questions.q: What is Machine Learning?
options: A computer that follows only hand-written rules
A type of AI where the computer learns patterns from examples
A physical robot brain
A programming language
questions.explanation: Machine Learning allows a computer to learn patterns directly from example data, instead of being given exact rules by a programmer.

questions.q: In simple terms, what is a 'model'?
options: The method used to train the AI
The raw data used for training
The output produced after training, containing the learned patterns
The question a user asks
questions.explanation: A model is the result of the training process. It stores the learned patterns and is used to generate predictions.

questions.q: What is the difference between training and inference?
options: Training uses the model; inference builds it
Training is when the model learns; inference is when it produces answers
They are the same process
Inference happens before training
questions.explanation: Training is the learning phase, where the model is built. Inference is using that finished model to generate a response.

questions.q: Which type of learning uses examples that already include the correct answer?
options: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Random learning
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains a model using labeled data, meaning each example is paired with its correct answer.

questions.q: What does an 'embedding' do?
options: Encrypts the model file
Converts text or images into numbers that represent their meaning
Deletes training data
Speeds up network traffic
questions.explanation: Embeddings convert data such as text into numerical values, where items with similar meaning end up with similar numbers.

questions.q: What is a 'trust boundary'?
options: The maximum allowed size of a model
The line between what you control and what you don't
A specific type of firewall
A model's accuracy score
questions.explanation: A trust boundary separates trusted components you control from untrusted input coming from outside.

questions.q: Why is user input to an LLM a security concern?
options: It slows down the model
The model often cannot distinguish developer instructions from user text
It uses too much memory
It is always encrypted automatically
questions.explanation: LLMs process all text the same way by default, which means carefully crafted user input can override intended developer instructions.

questions.q: What is a 'hallucination' in an LLM?
options: When the model crashes
When the model confidently produces false information
When the model refuses to answer
When the model runs out of tokens
questions.explanation: A hallucination is a confident but incorrect response, since the model predicts likely patterns rather than verifying facts.

questions.q: What is a 'token'?
options: An API authentication key
A small unit of text that the model processes
A type of neural network
A complete training dataset
questions.explanation: Models break text down into tokens, small chunks of words, before processing it.

questions.q: What is 'data poisoning'?
options: Deleting a model's training data
Inserting malicious data into training to influence the model's behavior
Encrypting a dataset
Speeding up the training process
questions.explanation: Data poisoning involves inserting manipulated examples into the training data so the model learns behavior chosen by the attacker.

questions.q: Why should AI output be treated as untrusted?
options: It is always incorrect
It can contain attacks like XSS or SQL injection if used without validation
It takes too long to generate
It is encrypted by default
questions.explanation: AI-generated output can carry malicious content, so using it directly in browsers, database queries, or system commands is risky.

questions.q: What does the 'principle of least privilege' mean in the context of AI?
options: Give the AI as much access as possible
Give the AI only the minimum access it actually needs
Never let the AI respond to questions
Only use small models
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits what actions an AI system is allowed to take, reducing potential damage if it is ever manipulated.

questions.q: What is 'indirect prompt injection'?
options: Typing a command directly into a chatbot
Hiding malicious instructions inside external content the AI reads
Injecting SQL into a database
Overloading a model with too many requests
questions.explanation: Indirect prompt injection hides malicious instructions inside content like web pages, files, or emails that the AI later processes.

questions.q: What are 'parameters' (weights) in a model?
options: The questions users ask
The learned numeric values that store the model's knowledge
The name of the training algorithm used
The server's IP address
questions.explanation: Parameters are the numeric values inside the model that were adjusted during training and now hold what it learned.

questions.q: What is 'overfitting'?
options: The model learns general patterns effectively
The model memorizes training data instead of learning general patterns
The model is too small in size
The model runs faster than expected
questions.explanation: Overfitting means the model memorized its specific training data rather than learning generalizable patterns, and can sometimes even leak that data.

questions.q: What is the main risk of storing secrets in a system prompt?
options: It slows the model down
The secrets can often be extracted through clever input
It only increases token usage cost
There is no real risk
questions.explanation: System prompts can frequently be extracted by attackers, so any secret stored there is at risk of being exposed.

questions.q: What is the 'attack surface'?
options: A model's accuracy score
Every possible point where an attacker could try to gain access
The physical size of the server
The total training time
questions.explanation: The attack surface refers to the complete set of entry points an attacker could potentially target.

questions.q: Which of these should be treated as an untrusted source for an AI system?
options: A web page the AI is asked to read
The developer's own verified configuration file
Both should be trusted equally
Neither should be trusted
questions.explanation: External content such as web pages is untrusted and can contain hidden malicious instructions.

questions.q: What does 'defense in depth' mean?
options: Relying on one very strong defense
Stacking multiple layers of defense so a single failure doesn't compromise the whole system
Only securing the database
Disabling the AI system entirely
questions.explanation: Defense in depth combines multiple layers of protection, so an attacker has to bypass all of them, not just one, to succeed.

questions.q: Which statement is true about AI models?
options: They truly understand meaning the way humans do
They predict patterns and can produce confident but incorrect answers
They are impossible to trick
Safety training alone makes them fully secure
questions.explanation: Models predict likely patterns based on training data rather than truly understanding content, and their safety behavior can always be challenged by a determined attacker.
